newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech leaders agree to consider cabinet shakeup.
newsitem.headline: Czech leaders agree to consider cabinet shakeup.

text.p: The Czech cabinet appeared headed for a shakeup on Tuesday as Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) agreed to discuss changes with its two partners in the ruling centre-right coalition.
"(The ODS leadership) expressed its agreement with the opening of a debate on the reconstruction of the government with our coalition partners," Klaus said in an interview on Czech Radio.
The Czech news agency CTK quoted ODS deputy chairman Miroslav Macek as saying that the cabinet changes should be completed by the end of June.
Later, government spokesman Ivo Strejcek told Reuters that leaders of the coalition parties might meet on Tuesday afternoon or evening.

Klaus's government has come under fire in recent weeks because of a slowdown in the country's economic performance, some highly publicised cases of financial crime as well as problems in the health care and education sectors.

Macroeconomic problems -- mainly a current account deficit of more than nine percent of gross domestic product and falling industrial output -- have cut the value of the crown on foreign exchange markets.
The crown has also been hit by worries about political instability. The central bank intervened several times last week to support it.
Opinion polls show support for Klaus's centre-right ODS at a record low. Support for the opposition Social Democrats has climbed well above that for the three parties in the ruling coalition.
Thirty five percent of respondents in a poll released on Monday said they trusted the government, down from 38 percent in April and 47 percent a year ago.
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik was chiefly blamed for the country's problems in the poll on Monday, with 28 percent saying he should resign.
Second in the unpopularity stakes was Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy with 22 percent saying he should quit.
Eighteen percent said Klaus should go.

Last month, Klaus announced a package of measures aimed at giving fresh impetus to economic growth, curbing trade and current account deficits and clamping down on economic crime. It included cuts in public spending and limits on wage growth.

"The ODS's declining popularity probably also means that the public has not embraced the package of measures that the government recently announced in an effort to correct negative economic developments," independent political analyst Jiri Pehe said.
"As the package was not accompanied by radical personal changes in the government it is now backfiring and, once again, affecting adversely mainly the ODS," he added.
